theme: The just shall live by faith, wrestling with God’s ways
readingInstruction: Read Habakkuk 1:1-3:19. Habakkuk does something unusual for a prophet: he argues with God. Read it as a conversation. Notice how the prophet’s questions change, and where the book ends.
settingTheScene: Habakkuk prophesied in Judah around 610 to 600 BC, probably in the days of King Jehoiakim, when the Assyrian empire was collapsing and Babylon was rising. Judah was full of violence and injustice. Habakkuk cries out to God, and God’s answer disturbs him even more. The book is a dialogue between a troubled believer and a sovereign God. It ends with one of the greatest expressions of faith in the Bible.
observation: “O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? Or cry to you Violence! and you will not save?” (1:2).
“Look among the nations, and see; wonder and be astounded. For I am doing a work in your days that you would not believe if told” (1:5).
“For behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans” (1:6).
“You who are of purer eyes than to see evil and cannot look at wrong, why do you idly look at traitors?” (1:13).
“I will take my stand at my watchpost… and look out to see what he will say to me” (2:1).
“Behold, his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith” (2:4).
“For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea” (2:14).
“Though the fig tree should not blossom… yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation” (3:17-18).
interpretation:
Habakkuk’s first complaint is that God is silent in the face of violence in Judah. God answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans, the Babylonians, a fierce and dreadful nation. This is not the answer Habakkuk wanted. He asks a second question: How can a holy God use a nation more wicked than Judah to punish them? “You who are of purer eyes than to see evil… why do you look at traitors and remain silent when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he?” It is an honest, hard question about God’s justice and his ways.

Habakkuk then takes his stand like a watchman and waits. God replies, and tells him to write the vision plainly. It will surely come, though it seems slow. And at the center of the answer is the verse that changed history: “The righteous shall live by his faith.” The proud, puffed-up man depends on himself. The righteous person depends on God, and lives by trust in him, even when the answer seems to be delay.

The rest of chapter 2 contains five woes against the Babylonians, those who plunder, build their house by injustice, build cities with blood, make others drunk, and trust in idols. They will fall. “But the LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him.” It is a verse that stills the questions.

Chapter 3 is a prayer, set to music, that recalls God’s great acts in the exodus and at Sinai. Habakkuk sees God coming in splendor, with light and pestilence. He trembles. And then comes the glorious conclusion: “Though the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines… yet I will rejoice in the LORD.” He lists every kind of agricultural disaster, a picture of complete economic collapse. And still he rejoices. Faith does not depend on circumstances. “God, the Lord, is my strength; he makes my feet like the deer’s; he makes me tread on my high places.” The prophet who began in doubt ends in joy.
connection: Paul quotes Habakkuk 2:4 in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11, and the author of Hebrews quotes it in Hebrews 10:38. It became the foundation text of the Reformation. Habakkuk 2:14 echoes Isaiah 11:9. Romans 8:28 and 8:35-39 give a New Testament answer to Habakkuk’s questions: nothing can separate us from the love of God. Philippians 4:11-13 shows Paul’s contentment in every circumstance. James 1:2-4 calls us to count it joy when we meet trials.
application:
Bring your hardest question to God in prayer. Habakkuk shows that honest questions are welcome.

Take your “stand at the watchpost.” Set aside time to listen after you have prayed.

Write out your own version of Habakkuk 3:17-18, naming real things that could be taken from you, and say you will still rejoice in the LORD.
prayerPrompts: Ask him to teach you to live by faith.
Tell him you will rejoice in him even when things are barren.
